newsitem.title: UK: BA warns time running out for American deal.
newsitem.headline: BA warns time running out for American deal.

text.p: British Airways Plc threatened on Wednesday to abandon its proposed alliance with American Airlines, and with it support for an Anglo-U.S. open skies aviation trade deal, if regulatory approvals did not come through before November.

"It is really up to the authorities to decide whether they want consumers to enjoy the benefits of open skies and more competition at Heathrow (airport) that this deal will bring," a company spokesman said.

He was confirming remarks made by BA chief executive Robert Ayling in an interview with the Financial Times published on Wednesday that he wanted the deal approved by November, when the world airline industry routinely meets to agree allocations of runway slots at busy airports for next year's summer season starting in April.
"After that it becomes more difficult," Ayling said. "There comes a point in any transaction where not having approval is tantamout to being told 'no'."

"There are some key dates," company spokesman David Budgens said. "The November slot conference is one which we need to take into account in planning for the launch of the alliance. We cannot wait forever," he said.
But Budgens also pointed out that Ayling said in the interview that he was hopeful the regulatory process was picking up again after last month's election in Britain.
"Obviously while it is true that we have become frustrated at the time that it has taken to win approval we want this deal done," the spokesman said.
"There are signs of movement in Washington, Whitehall and in Brussels and we are still hopeful that the alliance can proceed," he added.
It is exactly a year ago today that BA and American announced their alliance, but they are still struggling to win approvals in the U.S. and Europe in the face of fierce opposition.
Under the proposed alliance, BA intends to co-ordinate its 244 flights a week to 22 U.S. destinations with American's 238 flights from seven U.S. airports to 12 European destinations.

Rival airlines, the European Union's Competition Commissioner and consumer groups have all objected to the deal, alleging that it would dominate Europe's biggest trans-Atlantic market and lead to higher fares.
But BA and American say their deal would lead to greater competition, not less, because it would allow all U.S. airlines access to compete at Heathrow, Europe's most important transatlantic landfall.

Both Britain and the U.S. has made approval of the alliance conditional on Britain and the U.S. agreeing to liberalise the transatlantic market with an open skies pact, which requires Britain to open up London Heathrow to greater competition.
But no date has been set for resumption of open skies talks between the two countries, which were interrupted by last months change of government in Britain.
Adding to the delays, EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said last week that he did not expect the Commission to rule on the deal before September.
Under the current Bermuda II bilateral treaty, only four airlines can operate transAtlantic services out of Heathrow -- BA, American, UAL Corp's United Airlines and Virgin Atlantic Airways.

But rival airlines want BA and American to be forced to surrender some of their own runway slots at Heathrow to make room for the new competition, while BA and American contend that enough slots would be available.
Ayling and American's chairman Robert Crandall were due to take their case back to Washington today with an appearance before the House of Representatives' aviation committee.
